did_you_know.text: Isaiah describes the death of the righteous as an event the generation does not notice, explaining that the righteous are taken away "FROM THE EVIL".
The next verse presents the rest of the righteous after death: "He shall enter into peace," and they will rest on their beds because they walked in the way of righteousness.
The prophet addresses those who practice sin and idolatry in words of rebuke, describing them as "children of divination" and "offspring of an adulterer."
Isaiah mentions forbidden rituals performed beneath trees and in the valleys, and even describes the sacrifice of children as one of the sins he condemns.

The prophet describes idolatry in the valleys of the land: the stones and objects in the valley became, in his words, "your portion" and "your lot," and drink offerings and grain offerings were presented to them.
The chapter uses images of oil, fragrances, and perfumes to describe the nation's appeals to foreign powers; as a result, it is brought low, even to Sheol.
Isaiah contrasts the gathered idols, which cannot save and will disappear like the wind, with the one who takes refuge in the LORD, who will inherit the land and possess His holy mountain.
The chapter emphasizes that despite the LORD's exalted nature, He also dwells with the crushed and humble in spirit, to revive the spirit and heart of the oppressed.
The LORD declares peace and healing both to the "far" and to the "near," emphasizing the breadth of the comfort and healing He provides.
The wicked are compared to a stormy sea that cannot become calm, whose waters churn up mud and dirt; therefore the chapter concludes: "There is no peace... for the wicked."
